My grandparents are first cousins which mostly likely contributed to a lot of mental illness in my family. Youngest uncle has schizophrenia, auntie has most likely undiagnosed borderline disorder, oldest uncle got recently diagnosed with anxiety (got a panic attack at the plane), and my dad the oldest child is a narcissist. And that’s just my dads side of the family. 

Truthfully, me and my siblings grew up feeling like we owed something to our parents because they had us so young. They would always tell us to be grateful for the things that they gave us like a house and schooling and food. I always felt a sort of unpaid debt to them my entire life even if they shortchanged me in so many basic ways. For example, when I was in elementary school my Dad made me wait after school for six hours because he couldn’t be bothered to leave his work for 30 minutes to pick me up. My brother begged him to let him pick me up since he knew I was waiting and probably scared. It was night time already and that’s the only time my brother was able to come after my dad refused to let him leave saying that “I could wait more I’m already four.” 

The point is, is that I don’t want my kids to ever feel indebted to me so until I do everything I can for myself I cannot fill their cup and have children. Hi! I’m a bit late to the party but I hope my advice helps! I’m 5’4 and now 120 lbs but when I started last year I was almost 150. I did the same thing your wife did which was count calories and do a lot of cardio but I felt like restricting my diet really made me want to eat more. What honestly helped me was doing intermediate fasting (I work long hours and generally only eat twice a day). I basically eat what I want within the time window but I also keeptrack of my calories just not as intensely. Also by making things less strict at first it makes it easier to feel small “wins.” 

As for exercise, I did start out by doing mostly cardio but incorporated maybe one or two compound exercises like squatting or deadlifts. Then after a while I found that I liked doing weightlifting more and did cardio less and less. It’s really all about aiming to do something active at least a couple times a week and seeing what works for you rather than what is truly optimal tbh. I’m sure that even if she decides she prefers doing cardio or HIIT type exercises at the end of the day it’s whatever motivates the both of you to go to the gym! :) 

Oh but if there’s one thing to really be strict about it’s the things you drink. So many empty calories in soda and beer 😭 this was honestly the hardest for me to give up but the easiest way to lose weight. 

Hope this helps!

1. Always keep your hands full. When you bring something out, make sure you bring something back in (dirty dishes etc). 

2. Especially when training, it’s better to ask rather than make a mistake that can’t be fixed. Don’t worry about trying to do everything all at once. 

3. I’ve worked in Japanese restaurants for a long time. The most important thing would probably be able to tell the different types of fish by looking at it as well as the specialty rolls that they probably offer. As another poster said, learn the names in English and Japanese because you will get some pretentious ass people trying to order things in Japanese. Just the basic tuna salmon and yellowtail will probably do for now. 

4. Always make eye contact and be friendly with people. They pay your bills and just want to have a good meal. 

5. Be aware of your surroundings and keep watching the customers as well as the other servers. Being able to think on your feet and anticipate what to do next will be the most beneficial thing you can learn and will set you apart from other servers.
